evidence.evidence_text: Officially dedicated and opened on February 12, 1930, this historic masonic temple was recognized as a National Historic Site of Canada in 2001, celebrated for its elegant Beaux-Arts architecture. The concept of the Memorial Temple emerged as a tribute to Freemasons who lost their lives during World War I, replacing an earlier Masonic Temple situated in a mixed-use building on Dorchester Street since 1895.

Officially dedicated and opened on February 12, 1930, this historic masonic temple was recognized as a National Historic Site of Canada in 2001, celebrated for its elegant Beaux-Arts architecture. The concept of the Memorial Temple emerged as a tribute to Freemasons who lost their lives during World War I, replacing an earlier Masonic Temple situated in a mixed-use building on Dorchester Street since 1895.

In December 1930, the journal Construction highlighted the temple's architectural excellence, comparing it favorably to renowned works by architects such as McKim, Mead and White, and praising it alongside other notable structures like the Lincoln Memorial and the J.P. Morgan Library. One year later, the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada awarded its First Award, Class I, for Monumental Buildings to the Montreal Masonic Memorial Temple.
